title: Indian-American Educator Pia Dandiya Wins Florida Democratic Primary, Setting Up November Battle for Congress
excerpt: The first-generation Indian-American, a former White House Fellow and Harlem school founder, will face Republican Casey Askar in the newly drawn 22nd Congressional District.
body:
• Pia Dandiya, 39, won the Democratic primary for Florida's 22nd Congressional District on Tuesday, defeating Kaysia Earley to secure the nomination.
  • Dandiya is a first-generation Indian American, Harvard graduate, former White House Fellow, and founder of a public charter high school in Harlem.
  • She will face Republican Casey Askar in the November 3 general election in a newly redrawn district that spans parts of Palm Beach and Broward counties.
  • The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has added Dandiya to its Red to Blue program, signaling the party views the seat as competitive.

Dandiya Secures Democratic Nomination

Pia Dandiya won the Democratic primary for Florida's 22nd Congressional District on Tuesday, advancing to what both parties expect will be one of the more closely watched House races of the 2026 cycle. The 39-year-old educator and former White House Fellow defeated Kaysia Earley to claim the nomination.

"Tonight, high school principal, teacher, mom, and FL-22 congressional candidate Pia Dandiya won the Democratic primary election," her campaign said in a statement. Dandiya thanked voters "who joined this movement to lower costs, end corruption, and make Washington actually work for us."

"I've worked in the classroom and the principal's office, and I know what it takes to show up for people every single day, not just when it's convenient."

— Pia Dandiya, in her victory statement

From Delhi Slums to the Halls of Congress

Dandiya's trajectory reads like a case study in diaspora ambition. The daughter of Bharati Dandiya, founder of the Turtle River Montessori School in Jupiter, Florida, she grew up as a first-generation Indian American. She earned a BA in Government from Harvard University, where she interned for Senator Bill Nelson, and later completed a Master of Education from Boston University.

During her undergraduate years, she volunteered in New Delhi, teaching English to children in underprivileged communities — an experience she has said shaped her commitment to educational equity. After college, she served as an AmeriCorps member in the greater Boston area and worked as a Manager of Teacher Leadership Development for Teach For America.

At 28, Dandiya founded a public charter high school in Harlem, becoming one of the youngest principals in the United States. Every graduating student from the school earned college admission, despite most coming from low-income backgrounds. She later served as a White House Fellow from 2020 to 2021, working with the Domestic Policy Council and the Department of Education, before joining Apple to work on public sector initiatives involving education, healthcare, and government systems.

A Competitive District Takes Shape

The race was created when Governor Ron DeSantis signed a new congressional map that left the district without an incumbent. The newly drawn District 22 covers Wellington and the western stretches of Boynton Beach and Delray Beach, then runs south into Broward County and west toward Florida's Gulf Coast.

On the Republican side, Casey Askar won a crowded primary that included seven candidates. The district leans Republican under the new lines — about 55% of voters backed Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election — but Democrats point to modeling showing Joe Biden would have carried the same geography with 51% of the vote in 2020.

The DCCC added Dandiya to its Red to Blue program ahead of the primary, a signal that national Democrats view the seat as winnable. "While Republicans attempted to gerrymander South Florida to distract from their trail of broken promises, Pia stepped up to serve working people," DCCC Chair Rep. Suzan DelBene said.

What Dandiya Is Running On

Dandiya's campaign is organized around three pillars: lowering the cost of living by creating jobs and making housing, childcare, healthcare, and insurance more affordable; strengthening public education through investments in universal pre-K, K-12 schools, higher education, and workforce development; and protecting economic security by safeguarding Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and reproductive rights.

She has raised more than $2 million for her campaign, with $1.37 million in cash on hand as of June 30, according to Federal Election Commission filings — a strong war chest for a first-time congressional candidate in a mid-cycle race.

"Few districts feel the combined effects of cost-of-living increases and climate impacts as directly as this one," Dandiya said in her campaign questionnaire. She has highlighted South Florida's property insurance crisis and the compounding effects of rising seas, chronic flooding, and stronger storms on household budgets.

What's Next

The general election is scheduled for November 3. Indian American Impact, a national organization focused on increasing South Asian representation in government, congratulated Dandiya on her win. If she prevails in November, Dandiya would add to a small but growing cohort of Indian-American members of Congress that includes Representatives Ro Khanna, Raja Krishnamoorthi, and Pramila Jayapal, along with Senator Amish Shah, who is running his own competitive race in Arizona.
